events.description:

__________________________________________________________________

The language of psychoanalysis proliferates in modernist literature. In Freud’s work on sexuality, unconscious motivation and the fragmentation of memory, he developed a worldview that seemed to encompass the anxieties inherent in the experience of the early 20th century subject. This worldview also became the concern of modernist literature, with many of its leading figures consciously or unconsciously operating under the conceptual landscape first plotted by the founder of psychoanalysis.

This course explores the relationship that key figures in the history of literary modernism had with Freud, from often polarised perspectives. Reading key psychoanalytic texts alongside the works of Mann, Proust, Joyce and others, we will discover how Freud’s discoveries helped to animate the innovations in both form and content that mark this period of literature.

events.title: Freudian Research Seminar – The Dead That Answer Back: Conversational AI, Mourning and the Production of Posthumous Presence
events.description:
All registrants will receive their link to join via ZOOM. Attendees will also receive access to the recording on the Monday after the event, available to watch back for 3 months.

________________________________________________________________________

Abstract:
What happens when the dead no longer only leave traces, but appear to answer back?

This paper examines conversational AI as an emerging apparatus for mourning, projection and the production of posthumous subjectivity. Digital legacy has generally been framed through the logic of remains: profiles, photographs, messages, passwords, archives and memorialised accounts. Generative AI unsettles this framework by transforming traces into responsive outputs. The dead are no longer only preserved as digital objects; they may be encountered as simulated interlocutors.

The paper develops the concept of digital dialogic inheritance to describe the afterlife of a relation between a person and an AI system. Such inheritance is not made only of stored information, but of repeated exchanges, corrections, refusals, linguistic habits and recognisable forms of thought. Over time, the system does not simply learn what a person says; it may learn what they would reject, reformulate or refuse to become.

This argument is explored through What (A)I am after me, a speculative and auto-ethnographic experiment based on a long-term conversational relation with AI. The experiment asks what happens when this relation is imagined after death, once the person who corrected, interrupted and redirected the system can no longer intervene. Three figures encounter the traces that remain: a husband, a media theorist and a future relative who never knew her. Each produces a different version of posthumous presence through grief, critique or mediated familiarity.

Drawing on digital afterlife studies, media theory and psychoanalytic questions of mourning, fantasy and the uncanny, the paper argues that posthumous AI does not simply simulate the dead. It reorganises the relation between absence and response. Its most disturbing promise is not resurrection, but the possibility that loss may become interactive.

_______________________________________________________________________

Speaker:

Ilaria Iacconi Iambrenghi works across spatial research, communication and critical sociological studies, focusing on how physical, digital and symbolic spaces produce power relations, inequalities and forms of belonging. Her work has been presented in international, academic and professional contexts including UN-Habitat, the World Health Organization, the UIA World Congress of Architects, the UIA Public Health Group, Sapienza University of Rome, IUAV University of Venice, the University of Siena, Birzeit University, the Italian National Institute of Urban Planning (INU), and the Italian Political Science Association (SISP). In 2024 she founded cris&s – Centre for Research on Intersectional Spaces and Societies, a research platform dedicated to studying space as a structural condition of permanent crisis.

________________________________________________________________________

From care crisis to care stripping: building care in times of despair

Celebrating The Care Manifesto: The Politics of Interdependence, 2nd edition.

 

Despite widespread interest in our Care Manifesto, since its publication we have seen not a growing embrace of the politics of care, but, rather, an intensification in the politics of carelessness and cruelty. Indeed, over the past half decade, the world has witnessed continued warfare, mass human destruction, the amassing of ever more obscene wealth by the few, ongoing austerity, and ‘care-stripping’. Yet even in these times of despair, there is also evidence of increased grassroots resistance and support for better lives for all, as seen, for example, in the popularity of Mamdani in New York and Claudia Sheinbaum in Mexico. In these harsh times, we return to the premises of The Care Manifesto and ask how we can collectively strengthen our notions and practices of care? We argue that placing care front and centre of our politics is even more urgent today than it was when the first edition of the manifesto was published six years ago.

Please click here if you would like to purchase an in-house ticket.

 

About the book:

The Care Manifesto is the fiercely argued demand to place care at the centre of our politics. Our lives are always interdependent. It is by nurturing these ties that we cultivate a world in which every one of us can not only survive but thrive. Care must be at the heart of the state and the economy, promoting collective joy, not the satisfaction of individual desire. It should inform how we work, interact with each other, and plan our cities. It is part of how we can rebalance our relationship with the natural world.

__________________________________________________________________

Speakers:

Andreas Chatzidakis is Professor of Marketing and Consumer Ethics at the School of Business and Management, Royal Holloway, University of London. His works include The Moralizing Corporation; Gendering Marketing; Contemporary Issues in Marketing and Consumer Behaviour and Ethics and Morality in Consumption.

Jamie Hakim is a Senior Lecturer in Media and Cultural Studies at King’s College, London. He has published widely on queer cultures of embodiment, intimacy and care, including the books Work That Body and Digital Intimacies.

Jo Littler is Professor of Cultural, Media and Social Analysis at Goldsmiths, University of London. Her books include The Moralizing Corporation; Left Feminisms; Against Meritocracy; Radical Consumption; and The Politics of Heritage.

Catherine Rottenberg is Professor of Media, Communications and Cultural Studies at Goldsmiths, University of London. Her books include The Rise of Neoliberal Feminism, This is Not A Feminism Textbook! Performing Americanness, and Black Harlem and the Jewish Lower East Side. She is currently working on a co-authored book entitled Feminism Against Fascism.

Lynne Segal is Professor Emerita of Psychology & Gender Studies at Birkbeck, University of London. Her books include Beyond the Fragments (co-authored); Is the Future Female?; Slow Motion: Changing Masculinities, Changing Men; Straight Sex; Why Feminism?; Out of Time: The Pleasures and perils of Ageing; Radical Happiness: Moments of Collective Joy; Lean on Me: The Politics of Radical Care.

events.title: Freud Museum Reading Group – Civilisation and its Discontents
events.description:
Civilisation and its Discontents has remained one of Freud’s best loved and most widely read works ever since its publication in 1930. Taking as its theme, the relationship between the ‘progress’ of civilisation and an increase in human unhappiness, Freud’s brilliantly unpacks how technological and cultural advances are in fact productive of anxiety and tension for the individual. Freud’s wide-ranging analysis leads to the most sustained application of drive theory, encompassing Eros and the death drive, that appears in his work. This allows him to shed new light on the nature of human aggression, and the origin of the sense of guilt. With its focus on the uneasiness which attaches to technological and cultural development, Civilisation and its Discontents is of vital importance to an understanding of the technological malaise and ecological anxieties that define the human condition in our current era.

The Freud Museum reading group is a unique opportunity to read Freud’s texts in a supportive and collaborative environment. We read texts line by line and discuss sections together.

His has recently written chapters on Psychoanalysis and the Detective Novel and Freud and Africa.

events.title: Lean on Me: Book Launch with Lynne Segal
events.description:
The Freud Museum London is delighted to host this evening event to celebrate the paperback release of Lynne Segal’s ‘Lean on Me’. On the night we will be joined by Lynne Segal and Akshi Singh to explore the themes of care, intimacy, and collective responsibility that are at the core of Lynne’s book.

Lynne and Akshi will discuss what it means to depend on one another in an age of social fragmentation, inequality and climate crisis, and consider how practices of radical care can help us imagine a more hopeful future.

________________________________________________________________________

About the book

Have you ever relied on the kindness of strangers? What brings people together to find hope and solidarity? What do we owe each other as citizens and comrades?

Questions of care, intimacy, education, meaningful work, and social engagement lie at the core of our ability to understand the world and its possibilities for human flourishing. In Lean On Me feminist thinker Lynne Segal goes in search of hope in her own life and in the world around her. She finds it entwined in our intimate commitments to each other and our shared collective endeavours.

Segal calls this shared dependence ‘radical care’. In recounting from her own life the moments of motherhood, and of being on the front line of second-wave feminism, she draws upon lessons from more than half a century of engagement in left feminist politics, with its underlying commitment to building a more egalitarian and nurturing world. The personal and the political combine in this rallying cry to transform radically how we approach education, motherhood, and our everyday vulnerabilities of disability, ageing, and enhanced needs.

Only by confronting head-on these different forms of interdependence and care can we change the way we think about the environment and learn to struggle — together —against impending climate catastrophe.

_______________________________________________________________________

Speakers:

Lynne Segal is Anniversary Professor Emerita of Psychology and Gender Studies in the Department of Psychosocial Studies at Birkbeck, University of London. She is the author of several titles, including Is the Future Female? Troubled Thoughts on Contemporary Feminism, Making Trouble: Life & Politics, Radical Happiness: Moments of Collective Joy, Out of Time: The Pleasures and perils of Ageing. Lynne Segal also co-wrote Beyond the Fragments: Feminism and the Making of Socialism with Sheila Rowbotham and Hilary Wainwright, and recently published Lean on Me: A Politics of Radical Care.

Akshi Singh is an associate editor at Parapraxis and deputy editor at Critical Quarterly, and is the editor of a special collection of Critical Quarterly presenting new writing on Marion Milner. She collaborates regularly with the Derek Jarman lab, and writes for the London Review of Books. Singh moved to the UK from India to study for a PhD in psychoanalysis and literature with Jacqueline Rose. She is currently training to be a psychoanalyst at the Centre for Freudian Analysis and Research.

The Freud Museum is delighted to welcome Salman Akhtar and Mary Kay O’Neill to discuss their edited volume, Anxiety: Clarification, Critique and Update. They will be joined in their discussion by the Freud Museum’s Research Manager and book contributor Tom DeRose.

The evening will begin with a presentation by Tom DeRose on Freud’s changing views on anxiety, considering the 100-year anniversary of the publication of Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety. Then Salman Akhtar will discuss the distinctions between different types of anxiety and their relations to fears and phobias. Finally, Mary Kay O’Neill will discuss the theme of the professional anxieties of analysts. There will be opportunities for audience questions and discussion throughout the event.

Please click here if you would like to purchase an in-house ticket.

About the book:

Anxiety is one of the most central concepts in both the theoretical and clinical foundations of psychoanalysis. Thus, the study of anxiety is, in effect, the study of psychoanalysis itself. Salman Akhtar and Mary Kay O’Neil have gathered together a thoughtful group of scholars to cover this challenging terrain. The book opens with two chapters that lay out the groundwork for things to come: the first offers succinct definitions of the plethora of psychiatric and psychoanalytic terms pertaining to this emotion; the second elucidates Freud’s changing views of anxiety. These chapters are followed by independent discourses on separation anxiety and castration anxiety that attempt to describe, critique, and update these well-established notions. A section on cultural matters follows which includes essays on performance and climate anxieties. Part IV focuses on the clinical process and provides three pithy discourses on the entanglement of anxiety with enactment, aging, and trauma. The fifth and final part explores the analyst’s clinical and professional anxieties.

__________________________________________________________________

Speakers:

Salman Akhtar was born in India and completed his medical and psychiatric education there. Upon arriving in the USA in 1973, he repeated his psychiatric training at the University of Virginia School of Medicine, and then obtained psychoanalytic training from the Philadelphia Psychoanalytic Institute. He is Emeritus Professor at Jefferson Medical College and a training and supervising analyst at the Psychoanalytic Center of Philadelphia. He has authored, edited or co-edited more than 118 books on psychiatry and psychoanalysis, including his most recent: Freud in Istanbul: Turkish contributions to Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis. He is also a Scholar-in-Residence at the Inter-Act Theatre Company in Philadelphia. Salman Akhtar received the Sigourney Award in 2012.

Mary Kay O’Neil is supervising and training psychoanalyst of the Canadian Institute of Psychoanalysis and a registered psychologist in private practice in Toronto. She is a member of the TIP Curriculum Committee and of the Centre for Advanced Psychoanalytic Studies, and formally North American representative on the IPA Board. She has served on a number of local, national and international committees and on the editorial board of the International Journal of Psychoanalysis. She is also the author of several books, including The Unsung Psychoanalyst: The Quiet Influence of Ruth Easser, and Mothering Alone: A Plea for Opportunity.

Tom DeRose is Research Manager at the Freud Museum London. His research focusses on the cultural and philosophical aspects of Freudian theory. His most recent publication is ‘Freud’s Changing Views on Sadomasochism’, published in, ed. Akhtar and Crilley, ‘The Joy of Torment’ (Karnac, 2024). His has recently written chapters on Freud’s theory of Anxiety and Psychoanalysis and the detective novel, and is currently working on a chapter on Freud and Africa.

events.title: Freud’s Afternoon Session – Greek Myths for a Post-truth World
events.description:
What can ancient Greek myths teach us about the troubles and challenges of our post-truth times: environmental degradation, mass migration, war, inequality, exclusion, authoritarianism, and perplexing technological possibilities? Using some of his favourite myths as points of departure, Yiannis Gabriel will invite the audience to think and experience the world we inhabit mythologically – to engage with emotions and symbolism that lurk deeply inside old texts and to consider different courses of action, individual and collective, they open up. In addition to acting as fountains of meaning when meaning is precarious and fragmented, Greek myths, he will argue, have a therapeutic power helping us face the future with greater fortitude and practical wisdom that we so badly need in our times.

Yiannis Gabriel, a Greek social psychologist, is Professor Emeritus at Bath University, UK. As a Greek, he has had a life-long fascination with stories and myths which have played a large part in his research published in fourteen books, including Music and Story: A Two-Part Invention (2022), Myths, Stories, and Organizations: Premodern Narratives for Our Times (2004), Organizations in Depth: The Psychoanalysis of Organizations (1999) and Storytelling In Organizations: Facts, Fictions, and Fantasies (2000).

events.description:

The Freud Museum London is delighted to welcome acclaimed novelist Chloe Aridjis following the Booker Prize longlisting of her latest novel, The Shadow of the Object. Chloe Aridjis will be joined in conversation by writer and critic Devorah Baum.

Drawing on questions of memory, desire, loss and the mysterious lives of things, The Shadow of the Object explores the emotional and psychological traces that objects leave behind. In a conversation following the novel’s preoccupations, Aridjis and Baum will discuss the novel’s engagement with memory, fantasy and the unconscious, considering how objects, images and acts of looking become charged with emotional significance. Together, they will also reflect on the relationship between psychoanalysis and fiction, and how they inform each other.

 

About the book:

Flora is visiting home in Mexico when the family dog leaps up and bites her hand. She winds up in hospital where she undergoes several surgeries under anaesthesia and meets Wilhelmina, an elderly German woman with pneumonia, who collects pre-cinema toys and instruments. The two of them embark on a series of dream-like conversations in the hospital corridors. Wilhelmina puts on a magic lantern show for Flora, leaving her spellbound.

When things take an unexpected turn, Flora finds herself entrusted with an important mission. She returns to London, where she resumes her job polishing silver at a jewellery shop, and strikes up a strange friendship with Wilhelmina’s son, Max. As Flora dips in and out of her imagination, she is increasingly aware it’s not only the magic lantern that projects, and her perception of reality is subtly altered.

events.title: Freudian Research Seminar – The Architecture of the Unconscious: Technology, Domestic Fantasy, and the Uncanny in Kane Parson’s ‘Backrooms’
events.description:
All registrants will receive their link to join via ZOOM. Attendees will also receive access to the recording on the Monday after the event, available to watch back for 3 months.

Abstract:
This paper offers a psychoanalytic and spatial reading of Kane Parsons’ Backrooms, arguing that the film reconfigures the Freudian uncanny (‘Das Unheimliche’) through the technological imagination of contemporary digital horror. Drawing on Gaston Bachelard’s (The Poetics of Space) concept of ‘topoanalysis’- the psychological study of the sites of intimate life- the paper argues that if Bachelard’s ‘topoanalysis’ studies the intimate spaces in which memory is housed, Backrooms imagines a pathological ‘topoanalysis’: a digital architecture in which memory, shame, and domestic fantasy are no longer sheltered but endlessly displaced.

Bachelard’s account of the house as a privileged site of intimacy, shelter, memory, and dreaming offers a productive framework for understanding the film’s central spatial disturbance. In Backrooms, however, this poetics of inhabited space is radically inverted. The doorway beneath Clark’s furniture showroom does not lead to a hidden refuge, but to an endless architectural system in which the promise of home is emptied, multiplied, and rendered uncanny. The showroom’s public image of domestic comfort and marital stability gives way to spaces that are repetitive, artificial, and impossible to inhabit.

The paper further considers the role of Mary, Clark’s psychotherapist, whose movement into the Backrooms literalizes the analyst’s attempt to enter the patient’s psychic space. Her passage transforms therapeutic listening into spatial investigation, as dream material and repressed affect become architectural form.

Finally, the paper situates Backrooms within the technological conditions of its emergence: online horror culture, found-footage aesthetics, and platform-born spectatorship. By bringing Bachelard’s spatial poetics into dialogue with Freud’s uncanny, the paper argues that Backrooms imagines the unconscious not simply as an interior depth, but as a digital architecture of dislodged habitation.

Panos Liakos is a MPhil researcher in Film Studies at the University of West London. His project examines the work of Yorgos Lanthimos through questions of household, exclusion, and cinematic genres. He holds an MA in Cinema Studies from New York University’s TISCH School of the Arts and has published film criticism in Greek and international outlets, including The National Herald and FilmBuff. events.title: IN PERSON – The Psychic Life of Fragments, with Raluca Soreanu
events.description:
This ticket is for IN-HOUSE access to this event. Please click here if you would like to purchase an online ticket.

________________________________________________________________________

The Freud Museum is delighted to host the book launch of Raluca Soreanu’s monograph ‘The Psychic Life of Fragments: On Splitting and the Experience of Time in Psychoanalysis’ (Routledge, 2026, The Relational Perspectives Series).

This evening symposium dedicated to the book (6:00pm – 8:00pm) is available either in person or online.

The Psychic Life of Fragments rethinks trauma and psychic fragmentation starting from the psychoanalytic clinic.

What does it mean to work with fragments in psychoanalysis? What is the psychic life of fragments? And what can a fragment do? Raluca Soreanu writes about trauma, fragmentation and the radical plasticity of the psyche. Reconstructing Sándor Ferenczi’s trauma theory, she articulates an original vocabulary of fractures, splits, atomisations, pulverisations, leakages, detritus and psychic dematerialisation along with new formations, protective membranes, expansions, contagions and growths. She approaches the scene of trauma from new angles, paying attention to oblique lines and asymmetric encounters. Mobilizing clinical and literary vignettes, this book further argues for a minor psychoanalysis, one that emerges at the intersection of four types of theoretical-clinical experimentation: a psychoanalysis of scars, a psychoanalysis of organs, an eventful psychoanalysis and a blue psychoanalysis.

This book is important for clinicians and trainees in psychoanalysis, for mental health practitioners working with trauma, and for psychosocial and psychoanalytic thinkers. It is written to be used, between the psychoanalytic chair and the couch, especially at challenging times, in the transference and in the world.

Please click here if you would like to purchase an online ticket.

 

About the book:

‘Raluca Soreanu has become an indispensable thinker in contemporary psychoanalysis. With dazzling precision, she shows that the psyche’s fragments are not detritus but lively actors in trauma, memory, and repair. This book outlines a ‘minor psychoanalysis’ of scars, organs, catastrophe—an audacious re-staging of Ferenczi that re-opens psychoanalysis to its most experimental, timely, and unruly possibilities.’

Patricia Gherovici, psychoanalyst and author of Transgender Psychoanalysis

‘Soreanu’s return to Ferenczi, like Lacan’s return to Freud, levers us not into the past but a transformational future, a new psychoanalytic imaginary that is oblique, tentacular, visceral, surreal, decolonial. Here is a vocabulary of pliable elements, mimicry, asynchronous temporalities, fluid bodies, mosaics of dead and alive fragments – a psyche sensorially gripped and dismembered by the scars of time, but endowed with radically creative capacities and modes of registration and survival. Compelling, poetic, and precise, anchored throughout in luminous clinical narratives and a rigorous didactic concern with process, this is an epoch-making contribution to the emergent Ferenczian tradition: rerouting the mainstream into fascinating, life-preserving waters.’

Matt Ffytche, Professor of Psychoanalytic Studies, University of Essex and Editor, Psychoanalysis and History

‘In her strikingly lyrical text, Raluca Soreanu elucidates what ‘being in fragments’ might mean psychically. Drawing on the work of Sándor Ferenczi, Soreanu takes us beyond the static and repetitive temporalities of dissociation and splitting, and suggests that rather than the discarded elements of trauma, psychic fragments have a life of their own. Through clinical vignettes she shows us how patient and analyst can create a montage of such fragments, producing transformations in suffering through the co-creation of new and surprising forms of psychic life. Breathtakingly original, Soreanu offers us an entirely new thesis on trauma.’

Lisa Baraitser, Psychoanalyst, The British Psychoanalytical Society, and Professor of Psychosocial Theory, Birkbeck, University of London, UK

 

On the evening:

During the symposium, introduced and moderated by Lizaveta van Munsteren, we will hear from the author, Raluca Soreanu, and from guest speakers G Lori Millon, Patricia Gherovici, Katie Gentile, Matt ffytche, Lisa Baraitser, Jakob Staberg, Laura Salisbury & Julianna Pusztai.

The Psychic Life of Fragments is part of the Relational Perspectives book series at Routledge, edited by Adrienne Harris, Eyal Rozmarin & Steven Kuchuck.

The evening symposium will be followed by a wine and canapés reception.

__________________________________________________________________

Speakers:

Raluca Soreanu is a psychoanalytic and psychosocial thinker and writer. She is Professor of Psychoanalytic Studies in the Department of Psychosocial and Psychoanalytic Studies, University of Essex, UK, and a psychoanalyst, member of the Círculo Psicanalítico do Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and of the Site for Contemporary Psychoanalysis, UK. She is the author of Working-through Collective Wounds: Trauma, Denial, Recognition in the Brazilian Uprising (Palgrave, 2018) and the co-author, with Jenny Willner and Jakob Staberg of Ferenczi Dialogues: On Trauma and Catastrophe (Leuven University Press, 2023). Her new book The Psychic Life of Fragments: On Splitting and the Experience of Time in Psychoanalysis was published by Routledge in April 2026 in the Relational Perspectives Series. She is the project lead of the FREEPSY: Free Clinics and a Psychoanalysis for the People: Progressive Histories, Collective Practices, Implications for Our Times (UKRI Frontier Research Grant), an interdisciplinary collective of ten researchers studying the histories and legacies of free psychoanalytic clinics around the world. She is Academic Associate of The Freud Museum London; and Editor of the Studies in the Psychosocial series at Palgrave and of the Important Little Books in Psychoanalysis Series at 1968 Press.

G Lori Millon is a psychoanalyst working in private practice in Bristol. They hold a professional doctorate in Counselling Psychology and they teach and sit on the Training Committee for the Society for Social and Critical Psychoanalysis. In 2018 G received the Rozsika Parker Prize for their writings on non-binary genders, and they recently completed the manuscript for a collection of psychoanalytic auto-theory essays entitled ‘Dreaming in Tongues’. G organises Heterotopia Bristol, a space for radical psychoanalysis that includes events, reading groups and a social dreaming rhizome.

Patricia Gherovici is a psychoanalyst and analytic supervisor. She is the recipient of the Mary Sigourney Award for her clinical and scholarly work with Latinx and gender-variant communities, and serves as a trustee of Pulsion: The International Institute of Psychoanalysis and Psychoanalytic Psychosomatics in New York. Her single-authored books include The Puerto Rican Syndrome (Gradiva Award; Boyer Prize), Please Select Your Gender, Transgender Psychoanalysis, and Bodies to Wear. She co-authored with Chris Christian Psychoanalysis in the Barrios: Race, Class, and the Unconscious (Gradiva Award; American Board and Academy of Psychoanalysis Book Prize). She has also co-edited with Manya Steinkoler, Lacan on Madness: Madness, Yes You Can’t; Lacan, Psychoanalysis and Comedy; Psychoanalysis, Gender and Sexualities: From Feminism to Trans* (Gradiva Award); and most recently, The Routledge International Handbook of Psychoanalysis and Gender.

Katie Gentile, Ph.D. is a practicing psychotherapist/analyst and Professor of Interdisciplinary Studies at John Jay College of Criminal Justice (CUNY). She is the author of Creating bodies: Eating disorders as self-destructive survival and The Business of being made: The temporalities of reproductive technologies, in psychoanalysis and cultures (Gradiva Award), both from Routledge. She is the editor of the journal Studies in Gender and Sexuality, on the faculty of New York University’s Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis and the Critical Social Psychology program at the CUNY Graduate Center. Her recent publications explore psychoanalysis as a more-than-human practice and the fetus as a fetish object to disavow climate catastrophe. She is an active violinist who has recorded, toured, and plays with a number of bands and an avid open-water swimmer.

Matt ffytche is Professor at the Department of Psychosocial and Psychoanalytic Studies, University of Essex, and his publications include The Foundation of the Unconscious: Schelling, Freud and the Birth of the Modern Psyche (2011). He is editor of the journal Psychoanalysis and History, and an Academic Associate of the British Psychoanalytical Society.

Lisa Baraitser is a psychoanalyst in practice in London (Member of the British Psychoanalytical Society) and Professor of Psychosocial Theory in the School of Social Sciences at Birkbeck, University of London. Her research is at the intersection between social theory, psychoanalysis, and gender and sexuality studies, and concerns the temporal, ethical and affective dimensions of care. She has written widely on feminist and psychoanalytic theory, motherhood, care and time. Her books include Maternal Encounters: The Ethics of Interruption (Routledge, 2009, joint-winner of the Feminist and Women’s Studies Association Book Prize); Enduring Time (Bloomsbury, 2017), the co-authored book, Waiting Times: Crisis, Chronicity and Care (Bloomsbury, 2026), and a forthcoming co-edited volume on Violence and the Feminine: Contemporary Psychoanalytic Perspectives which will be published by Routledge, co-edited with Emanuela Quagliata. From 2017-2023 Lisa was co-Principal Investigator of Waiting Times, a Wellcome Trust collaborative award leading a team of researchers to investigate the meanings of waiting in, and for healthcare. She is currently the Principal Investigator of a Wellcome Trust Discovery Award titled Contragestive Time: Pregnant Uncertainties in Fertility Control.

Jakob Staberg is a practicing psychoanalyst and psychotherapist, and member of the International Psychoanalytical Association. He is an assistant professor for Comparative Literature and lecturer in aesthetics at Södertörn, University South of Stockholm. Staberg is working in the field of aesthetics, literature and psychoanalytic theory. Staberg has devoted himself to the relationship between Freud and Ferenczi from the perspective of the problem of transference and as it is expressed in dream interpretation, he has published on this topic together with Raluca Soreanu and Jenny Willner, Ferenczi Dialogues: On Trauma and Catastrophe, Leuven University Press 2022. He has contributed in the anthology Towards the Limits of Freudian Thinking, Leuven University Press 2024 (ed Herman Westerink, Jenny Willner and Philippe van Haute). His forthcoming book, also published by Leuven University Press, is titled Aesthetics of Dreams: Shakespeare, Psychoanalysis and the Limits of Modernity.

Laura Salisbury is Professor of Modern Literature and Medical Humanities at the University of Exeter. Her work seeks to understand the relationship between time, care, and modes of narration. Laura has published widely on literary modernism, particularly the work of Samuel Beckett, and she is co-author of a new book about to be published by Bloomsbury: Waiting Times: Crisis, Chronicity and Care.

Julianna Pusztai is a London-based psychodynamic psychotherapist and psychosocial researcher, originally from Hungary. She has worked on several community projects, low-cost and free clinics, and is currently based at the Donald Winnicott Centre, East London NHS Foundation Trust. She is the co-founder of the Sándor Ferenczi Collective and a PhD candidate researching grassroots psychoanalytic collectives and DIY practices at Free Clinics and a Psychoanalysis for the People: Progressive Histories, Collective Practices, Implications for our Times [FREEPSY], University of Essex.

Lizaveta van Munsteren is a psychodynamic psychotherapist (BPC) and academic with a research focus in psychoanalytic theory and history. She is a lecturer in psychotherapy at King’s College London, and teaches Freud at the Bowlby Centre. She is also a postdoctoral researcher with the FREEPSY project at the University of Essex, UK, working on theoretical formulations of the psychoanalytic frame in free clinics, and archives of free clinics in Vienna and Budapest. Her book The Vicissitudes of Psychoanalysis in Soviet Russia, 1930-1980 was published with Routledge and Open Access in 2025.

She is the editor of the journal Studies in Gender and Sexuality, on the faculty of New York University’s Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis and the Critical Social Psychology program at the CUNY Graduate Center. Her recent publications explore psychoanalysis as a more-than-human practice and the fetus as a fetish object to disavow climate catastrophe. She is an active violinist who has recorded, toured, and plays with a number of bands and an avid open-water swimmer.

Matt ffytche is Professor at the Department of Psychosocial and Psychoanalytic Studies, University of Essex, and his publications include The Foundation of the Unconscious: Schelling, Freud and the Birth of the Modern Psyche (2011). He is editor of the journal Psychoanalysis and History, and an Academic Associate of the British Psychoanalytical Society.

Lisa Baraitser is a psychoanalyst in practice in London (Member of the British Psychoanalytical Society) and Professor of Psychosocial Theory in the School of Social Sciences at Birkbeck, University of London. Her research is at the intersection between social theory, psychoanalysis, and gender and sexuality studies, and concerns the temporal, ethical and affective dimensions of care. She has written widely on feminist and psychoanalytic theory, motherhood, care and time. Her books include Maternal Encounters: The Ethics of Interruption (Routledge, 2009, joint-winner of the Feminist and Women’s Studies Association Book Prize); Enduring Time (Bloomsbury, 2017), the co-authored book, Waiting Times: Crisis, Chronicity and Care (Bloomsbury, 2026), and a forthcoming co-edited volume on Violence and the Feminine: Contemporary Psychoanalytic Perspectives which will be published by Routledge, co-edited with Emanuela Quagliata. Jakob Staberg is a practicing psychoanalyst and psychotherapist, and member of the International Psychoanalytical Association. He is an assistant professor for Comparative Literature and lecturer in aesthetics at Södertörn, University South of Stockholm. Staberg is working in the field of aesthetics, literature and psychoanalytic theory. Laura has published widely on literary modernism, particularly the work of Samuel Beckett, and she is co-author of a new book about to be published by Bloomsbury: Waiting Times: Crisis, Chronicity and Care.

events.title: O pacto colonial da psicanálise e a violência contra a mulher
events.description:
A violência contra a mulher costuma ser abordada pela psicanálise, por um lado, como reação ao feminino, tomado como índice da castração, e, por outro, a partir do desamparo ou da dimensão pulsional implicada na violência.

Essa proposta parte de outra direção: perguntar em que medida as próprias categorias mobilizadas para pensar essa violência permanecem vinculadas a uma gramática patriarcal e colonial.

Quando gênero e raça são assumidos como operadores da crítica epistemológica, torna-se possível reconhecer que a pretensão de universalidade de certas formulações psicanalíticas pode pactuar epistemicamente com a violência contra a mulher.

Esse debate tomará esse impasse como ponto de partida para interrogar a própria psicanálise e considerar a função do ideal de masculinidade como uma via possível para abrir outros caminhos de reflexão sobre a violência contra a mulher.

Érico Andrade 

Psicanalista, filósofo, doutor em filosofia pela Sorbonne ( Paris IV). Professor Titular da Universidade Federal de Pernambuco. Pesquisador do Conselho Nacional de Desenvolvimento Científico e Tecnológico com bolsa de produtividade.

 

Thais Klein

Psicanalista, doutora em Teoria Psicanalítica (UFRJ), doutora em Saúde Coletiva (IMS-UERJ). Professora associada da Universidade Federal Fluminense. Professora do Programa de Pós-Graduação em Teoria Psicanalítica (UFRJ) e pós-doutoranda em Psicologia Clínica (USP) .

The Freud Museum is delighted to welcome acclaimed writer and critic Jacqueline Rose to mark the publication of her new novel, Two Women. Two Women is a fictional account tracing the lives and imagined interconnections of Edith Stein and Gillian Rose. Jacqueline Rose will be joined in conversation by fellow writer and critic Devorah Baum. Their discussion will explore the influence of psychoanalysis in the creative process particularly in connection with the novel, the relationship between biography and fiction, and how fiction can offer new ways of engaging with history and identity.

Please click here if you would like to purchase an in-house ticket.

 

About the book:

In Two Women, Jacqueline Rose fictionalizes and intertwines the lives of two remarkable figures whose stories trace the contours of the twentieth century: Edith Stein, the German-Jewish philosopher, Catholic convert and saint; and Gillian Rose, philosopher of German-Jewish thought, also a convert, and Jacqueline’s sister. Through a luminous weaving of fiction and history, Rose traces the parallels and distances between these women – their intellect, faith, suffering and courage – while also confronting the mysteries of love, loss and belonging that shape every human life. A deeply moving work, Two Women is at once an act of remembrance and a daring work of imagination by one of the most important feminist writers of our time.

Jacqueline Rose is internationally recognised as one of the most important living feminist critics. She is co-director of the Birkbeck Institute for the Humanities, co-founder of Independent Jewish Voices UK, a Fellow of the British Academy and of the Royal Society of Literature. She is a frequent contributor to the London Review of Books and New York Review of Books, The Guardian and other publications. Her books include States of Fantasy, The Last Resistance, Women in Dark Times, Mothers: an essay on love and cruelty, and The Plague: Living Death in Our Times. She is the recipient of the 2026 PEN Harold Pinter Prize.

Devorah Baum is Professor of English Literature at the University of Southampton. events.title: Inner Torment Part II: Fear, Hatred, Envy and Greed
events.description:
All registrants will receive their link to join via ZOOM. Attendees will also receive access to the recording on the Monday after the event, available to watch back for 3 months.

________________________________________________________________________

In the second instalment of his Inner Torment course, Professor Salman Akhtar will examine four more profoundly dysphoric internal experiences and their devastating psychosocial consequences. Each session will focus upon one such phenomenon and will offer illustrations from clinical experience, the literary realm, and day-to-day life. Each session will consist of a 60-minute talk and a 30-minute Q&A period, assuring a thorough engagement and participation by the audience.

 

Day One

Session I : Fear ……… This presentation will define fear and clarify its distinctions from anxiety. Universal fears will be listed and their diminution by helpful parental input ……deep thalamic apprehensions vs. their cortical corrections, in other words………will be highlighted. States of fearlessness and courage, as well as phobia and cowardice, shall be discussed. Clinical implications of all these proposals will be stressed.

Session II : Hatred ……… Hatred will be shown to be a complex characterological state with distortions of bot ego and superego functioning. Fantasies contributing to hatred will be underscored. Differences between rage and hate will be noted. Therapeutic strategies to deal with hate in transference and countertransference will be discussed with the help of ample clinical vignettes.

 

Day Two

Session III : Envy ……… Differences between Freud and Klein on the origins of envy will be highlighted. Distinction between envy and jealousy will be made, and defenses against the latter ( including narcissistic withdrawal contempt) will be highlighted. The role of envy in what Freud called ‘negative therapeutic reaction’ will be noted and its technical handling discussed.

Session IV : Greed ……… The phenomenon of greed will be deconstructed in its primary and secondary manifestations. The relationship between appetite, hope, desire, and greed will be discussed and so will be the defensive asceticism and pretended contempt for money that develops to ward of inner greed. Within the clinical situation, the patient’s greed for attention and the analyst’s greed for interpretation will be addressed.

________________________________________________________________________

Schedule:

This is a two-day online course occurring on both Wednesday 11th November and Wednesday 18th November, which will begin at 5pm and end at 9pm on both days with an allotted hour break.

__________________________________________________________________

Speaker:

Salman Akhtar, MD, was born in India and completed his medical and psychiatric education there. Upon arriving in the USA in 1973, he repeated his psychiatric training at the University of Virginia School of Medicine, and then obtained psychoanalytic training from the Philadelphia Psychoanalytic Institute. He is Emeritus Professor at Jefferson Medical College and a training and supervising analyst at the Psychoanalytic Center of Philadelphia. He has authored, edited or co-edited more than 118 books on psychiatry and psychoanalysis, including his most recent: Freud in Istanbul: Turkish contributions to Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis. He is also a Scholar-in-Residence at the Inter-Act Theatre Company in Philadelphia. Salman Akhtar received the Sigourney Award in 2012.

events.title: IN PERSON – Symposium & Book Launch of ‘Psychoanalysis Otherwise’ with Raluca Soreanu & Ana Minozzo
events.description:

________________________________________________________________________

The Freud Museum is delighted to host the launch of ‘Psychoanalysis Otherwise’, a collection edited by the FREEPSY Collective. This evening symposium is dedicated to the publication (6:00pm – 7:45pm), with the presence of editors Raluca Soreanu and Ana Minozzo, authors and guests. It is followed by launch of an exhibition by Ana Čvorović, curated by Sacha Craddock (8pm – 9pm), and a wine reception (9pm – 10pm). The symposium is available both in person and online.

The first part of the evening will be dedicated to the launch of Psychoanalysis Otherwise, a collection of papers by the Free Clinics Working Group (FCWG) at FREEPSY. The Free Clinics Working Group is a collective space of exchange, learning, thinking and writing promoted by FREEPSY.

Over the past four years, FREEPSY hosted guests from free clinics and scholars from various territories aiming at stretching our collective repertoire of what free psychoanalytic clinics are, can be and how they operate across different contexts.

Since 2022, the FCWG has been fostering the establishment of an intimate network of researchers & clinicians of psychosocial orientation that can discuss texts, think together and produce alternative types of scholarly work collectively such as zines, online dictionaries, artwork and essays. Psychoanalysis Otherwise is the fruit of these collective explorations.

On the evening, psychoanalysts Raluca Soreanu and Ana Minozzo will be in conversation with authors and guests, including Susana Caló and Anderson Santos.

The date also marks the first day of the three-week Free Clinics Festival, organised by the FREEPSY Collective. Held between November 16 and December 6 in various locations across London, the Free Clinics Festival includes a series workshops, book launches, conferences, artist talks, exhibitions and more. Please check the FREEPSY website for more information on how to register for the events: https://freepsyproject.com/fcf/.

The second part of the evening will be dedicated to the opening of an exhibition by Ana Čvorović, artist-researcher at FREEPSY, curated by Sacha Craddock. The exhibition will be displayed on site, at the Freud Museum, over the duration of the Free Clinics Festival.

The two launches will be followed by a reception.

Please click here if you would like to purchase an online ticket.

__________________________________________________________________

Speakers:

Susana Caló is a researcher and writer. Her work focuses on reconstructing potential histories of radical psy practices, considering their relationship to wider social, political and urban struggles with the aim to develop a critical theory of psychological practices and contemporary psychopolitics. Her most recent publication CERFI: Analysis Everywhere (Minor Compositions) is the result of ten years of collective research into the history and practices of French institutional analysis and psychotherapy, examining their conceptual and socio-political dimensions. She was a co-investigator in The Pragmatic Genealogy of Concepts (BA, King’s College London), examining the political life of concepts in post-war French thought. She is a founding member of Chaosmosemedia, a rhizomatic project that has organised several international events focusing on the work of the psychoanalyst and activist Félix Guattari. She lectures at the Open University and collaborates with the FREEPSY collective, acting as a consultant and network organiser contributing to the development of a Free Clinics Network.

Sacha Craddock (b. 1955) is an art critic, writer & curator based in London. She is co-founder of ArtSchool Palestine, member of Abbey Council, and co-founder of the Contemporary Art Award at the British School at Rome, Trustee of the Shelagh Cluett Trust, and President of AICA-UK. She was Chair of the Board of New Contemporaries and selection process from 1996 until 2021. Selected critical writing includes essays on Mark Boulos, Angus Fairhurst, Jose Dávila, Chantal Joffe, Wolfgang Tillmans, Rosa Lee, and Adam Henein, among others. She was the co-founder of Bloomberg Space and its curator from 2002-2011. Her curatorial contribution includes the Turner Prize, Hull 2017, Strike Site at Backlit Gallery, Nottingham 2018, Here, Now at Misk Art Institute 2021, Glossary for Curated by, Vienna 2023, and Thought to Image for Albion Jeune 2024. Latest curatorial projects include PLATAFORMA as International Guest Curator, Guadalajara 2025-2026, and David Garner: I have nothing to say only to show, Penarth 2025.

Ana Čvorović (b. Sarajevo 1981) is a contemporary artist based in London. Her installations are an exploration of the psychodynamics of place, specifically in the context of war, migration, and socio-economic impoverishment. Her solo exhibitions include Archipelago at Ballon Rouge, Brussels (2021) and Borders Unfold at Pi Artworks, London (2019). Recent residencies include Arthouse Jersey for the commissioned project No Place Like Home (2023); FAP, Lebanon (2022) supported by the Foundation for Art and Psychoanalysis; and Sculpture Space, New York (2018) supported by Arts Council England. She is an Artist Researcher on the UKRI-funded project FREEPSY: Free Clinics and a Psychoanalysis for the People at the University of Essex.

Ana Minozzo is a clinician and researcher based in London, UK. She holds a PhD and an MA in Psychosocial Studies from Birkbeck, University of London and is currently a Postdoctoral Researcher in Psychosocial Studies within FREEPSY, at the University of Essex (2023-2027). She has experience with a number of community-based mental health services, working with migrants, refugees, the LGBTQI+ community and was a part of the Psychosis Therapy Project, in London. Her research crosses the fields of medical humanities, feminism and psychosocial studies, with a special interest in ecofeminism and medical anthropology and has been featured in several edited books and journals internationally. Ana is a full member of The Site for Contemporary Psychoanalysis and a registered UKCP psychotherapist. Her book ‘Anxiety as Vibration: a Psychosocial Cartography’ was published by Palgrave in 2024.

Raluca Soreanu is a psychoanalytic and psychosocial thinker and writer. She is Professor of Psychoanalytic Studies in the Department of Psychosocial and Psychoanalytic Studies, University of Essex, UK, and a psychoanalyst, member of the Círculo Psicanalítico do Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and of the Site for Contemporary Psychoanalysis, UK. She is the author of Working-through Collective Wounds: Trauma, Denial, Recognition in the Brazilian Uprising (Palgrave, 2018) and the co-author, with Jenny Willner and Jakob Staberg, of Ferenczi Dialogues: On Trauma and Catastrophe (Leuven University Press, 2023). She is the project lead of the interdisciplinary research project FREEPSY: Free Clinics and a Psychoanalysis for the People: Progressive Histories, Collective Practices, Implications for Our Times (UKRI Frontier Research Grant); Academic Associate of The Freud Museum London; and Editor of the Studies in the Psychosocial series at Palgrave and of the Important Little Books in Psychoanalysis Series at 1968 Press. Her latest book is The Psychic Life of Fragments: On Splitting and the Experience of Time in Psychoanalysis.

Anderson Santos is an editor and organizer of the books Passagens por La Borde: clínica e instituição (Passages through La Borde: Clinic and Institution) (2026, cinco edições), Uma política da loucura e outros textos – François Tosquelles (A Politics of Madness and Other Texts – François Tosquelles) (2024, Sobinfluencia edições and ed. Ubu); Psicanálise e Esquizoanálise: diferença e composição (Psychoanalysis and Schizoanalysis: Difference and Composition) (2022, n-1 edições) among others. He holds a degree in Psychology, is a psychoanalyst, a member of the Coletivo Psicanálise na Praça Roosevelt, a specialist in ‘Saúde Mental, Imigração e Interculturalidade’ (Mental Health, Immigration and Interculturality) from the Federal University of São Paulo (UNIFESP), and holds a master’s degree in Health Sciences (UNIFESP).

events.title: ONLINE – Case by Case: Psychoanalysis and the Political Discourse | Book Launch with Patricia Gherovici & Jamieson Webster
events.description:
This ticket is for ONLINE access to this event. All registrants will receive their link to join via ZOOM. Attendees will also receive access to the recording on the Monday after the event, available to watch back for 3 months.

________________________________________________________________________

This event is part of the Free Clinics Festival organised by the FREEPSY Collective: https://freepsyproject.com/fcf/

Freud’s ‘talking cure’ and its offshoots are more widespread today than ever. But as the divisive issues of our time grow more urgent, a contentious question persists: must psychoanalysis remove itself from politics altogether in order to be effective? Or is it inherently political? Specific disagreements about how clinicians should or shouldn’t engage with imperialism, violence, race, and gender identity point to the broader question of where politics is situated in our psychic life. Is it on the periphery – a symptom or displacement – or right at the heart of the matter?

In this timely book, psychoanalysts Patricia Gherovici and Jamieson Webster examine the vexed relationship between psychoanalysis and politics through a sequence of case studies, exploring the many ways in which the political enters the consulting room. Ranging from early cases confronting homosexuality and race to idiosyncratic analyses disentangling the legacies of state and colonial violence, the authors illuminate how the political shapes our relationships to power, normativity, and identity. These historic cases are prescient of the political dilemmas confronting us today. Rather than dismissing psychoanalysis as irrelevant or reducing it to a vehicle for political positions, Case by Case makes a galvanizing and challenging argument for what psychoanalysis can reveal about our political selves – and how it might transform them.

events.title: Freudian Research Seminar – Capital, Delay, Body: Laura Mulvey’s Freud
events.description:
All registrants will receive their link to join via ZOOM. Attendees will also receive access to the recording on the Monday after the event, available to watch back for 3 months.

________________________________________________________________________

Abstract:
Considering three periods of her work, this talk will explore how Laura Mulvey has applied Freudian psychoanalysis to each of them, but more crucially will consider how Mulvey has used the technological changes of each historical moment to respond to and rethink Freud’s work. Beginning by briefly outlining Mulvey’s account of the relationship between the technology of the cinematic apparatus pre-1960 and Freudian fetishism, I then turn to the 1970s and Mulvey’s own experimental filmmaking practice with Peter Wollen, focusing on the ways in which the two drew on filmmaking technologies of the time to convey Freudian concepts through cinematic form – for instance, the ‘voice-off’ technique can be read as a response to Freud’s ‘Femininity’. Finally, the bulk of the talk will discuss Mulvey’s 2006 book Death 24x a Second, in which she examines then-recent technological changes including the rise of digital video and DVDs. She proposes that features such as pausing and rewinding enable a rethinking of concepts such as fetishism through, for instance, their ability to impose an artificial stillness.

The terms ‘capital,’ ‘delay,’ and ‘body’ are central to Mulvey’s 1977 film Riddles of the Sphinx. Nicolas Helm-Grovas has suggested ‘capital’ refers to Marxism and ‘body’ to psychoanalysis, with ‘delay’ being ambiguous. Delay, this talk suggests, shifts from initially referring to a critical distance vital to her socialist-feminist politics to later signifying retroactivity and deferral, and is considered a fundamental yet currently neglected term which indicates Mulvey’s repeated interest in rethinking Freudian philosophies of time through technological developments.

events.title: Freud’s Afternoon Session – Midlife
events.description:
“Throughout my therapeutic career most of my clients have been between the age of 35 and 55 and  arrive in the state of anxiety, overwhelmed by some intractable problem. We have come to call this the midlife crisis.” – Andrew Jamieson

Andrew Jamieson identifies that only two species of mammal have an extensive, post-reproductive life: killer whales – whose elders can sniff out food for their pods – and Homo sapiens. While the rationale behind the whale’s longevity seems clear, what is the point of ours? This question intrigued Carl Jung who observed that if a culture is to thrive, it must find a balance between the energy of the young and the experience of the old. But to obtain this equilibrium, we need to pass through the dreaded middle years. Examining the Jungian concept of the midlife crisis, and the lives of prominent figures who endured it (including Abraham Lincoln and Marie Curie), psychoanalyst Andrew Jamieson shows in his book how there is an evolutionary purpose behind this rite of passage which ­­– once traversed – holds the key to our prosperity.

The Freud Museum welcomes Andrew Jamieson for this Afternoon Session, in which Andrew will deliver a short presentation on his book, followed by a conversation with Dr Martin Gledhill.

_______________________________________________________________________

Speaker:

Andrew Jamieson is a psychotherapist based in Bath whose interests include psychotherapy’s interconnection with philosophy, music and literature. He is the author of Midlife: Humanity’s Secret Weapon and On the Couch: 20 extraordinary personalities from Picasso to Putin (both published by Notting Hill Editions). Parallel to his psychotherapeutic career, Jamieson has promoted orchestral concerts throughout the UK for over forty years.

Dr Martin Gledhill was a senior lecturer in the Bath University Architectural Department. He has always been fascinating by psychology and completed a PhD on the interface between architecture and psychology. Recently he has published a well received book on Jung’s Bollingen Tower and is currently working on a second book to be published by Routledge exploring further the overlap between psychology and architecture. He is the Chairman of the Trustees at the Bath Centre for Psychotherapy and Counselling.

After a serendipitous first meeting following a lecture, he has known Andrew Jamieson for a number of years. During enjoyably long walks in the Wiltshire and Somerset countryside they have discussed the many aspects of psychoanalysis and how it might aid our interpretation of an increasingly troubled world as much as ourselves.

events.title: Projections: Cinematic Representations of Mental Illness
events.description:
All registrants will receive their link to join via ZOOM. Attendees will also receive access to the recording on the Monday after the event, available to watch back for 1 month.

________________________________________________________________________

Cinema gives visible form to human experiences that are otherwise difficult to represent: anxiety as dread of an unformed threat, depression as a persistent loss of interest or pleasure, psychosis as a collapse of reality. Where clinical language classifies psychological disturbance, cinema makes it sensorial. It places us inside altered states of consciousness and asks us to observe what it might mean to lose one’s bearings.

This lecture examines how cinema has imagined emotional anguish across five distinct diagnostic categories: anxiety, depression, psychosis, obsessive compulsive disorder, and borderline personality disorder. We will explore the ways in which 10 films in particular depict various forms of distress through narrative, performance, sound, editing, colour, framing, and the treatment of time and space. Special attention will be given to the cultural preoccupations that these diagnoses carry (e.g., fear of losing control and instability of identity).

We will also consider cinema’s powerful role in shaping public ideas about mental illness. Films do not simply reflect societal attitudes towards psychological affliction, they actively participate in producing them. The figure of the ‘mad’ person has been variously constructed as victim, monster, genius, criminal, object of desire, and threat to social order. By examining these representations closely, we can distinguish between emotional reality and the cinematic fantasies projected onto it.

Advance viewing is optional; select scenes will be shown during the webinar.

events.title: Freudian Research Seminar – Psychoanalysis in the Digital Era
events.description:
All registrants will receive their link to join via ZOOM. Attendees will also receive access to the recording on the Monday after the event, available to watch back for 3 months.

________________________________________________________________________

Abstract:
The COVID-19 pandemic caused a major shift in psychoanalytic practice, requiring analysts around the world to move quickly from in-person sessions to remote work using telephone and video platforms. While this transition allowed treatment to continue, it also challenged traditional ideas about the analytic setting, presence, and the conditions needed for effective psychoanalysis. This study explores how psychoanalysts and psychoanalytic candidates experienced and understood remote analytic work during and after the pandemic.

Semi-structured interviews were conducted with twelve psychoanalysts and analytic candidates from different psychoanalytic backgrounds. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis guided by a psychoanalytic perspective, focusing on participants’ clinical experiences and reflections on remote treatment.

The findings indicate that remote psychoanalysis is not simply a weaker or equal version of in-person analysis, but a different form of analytic work with its own strengths and limitations. Participants reported changes in the experience of the analytic frame, transference and countertransference, embodiment, silence, intimacy, and the use of space. Rather than reducing unconscious communication, remote work appeared to change how unconscious processes were expressed and understood. Analysts emphasized the need for flexibility while maintaining core psychoanalytic principles and highlighted the importance of clinical judgment in deciding whether remote treatment is appropriate for each patient.

This study adds to the growing research on teleanalysis by providing a deeper psychoanalytic understanding of remote work beyond the immediate context of the pandemic. The findings suggest that psychoanalysis can adapt to changing circumstances while preserving its essential therapeutic values and encourage further exploration of how analytic practice may continue to evolve across different settings.

_______________________________________________________________________

Speaker:

Haroula (Charikleia) Ntalla is a New York State Licensed Psychoanalyst, Fellow of the International Psychoanalytical Association (IPA), and Clinical Professor at Brooklyn College, City University of New York. She is the founder and director of the Perinatal Mental Health Initiative at Brooklyn College, where she developed New York State’s first Advanced Certificate in Perinatal Mental Health. Her doctoral research at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis examines the experience of psychoanalysts working remotely during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, exploring how the analytic frame, embodiment, and unconscious communication are transformed in remote psychoanalytic treatment.

Abstract:
The widespread circulation of photographs through social media has transformed not only how images are consumed but also the psychic function of photography itself. Historically, photographs have been understood as objects of memory, preserving traces of people, places, and experiences that have passed. In contemporary digital culture, however, photographs increasingly appear to be created with their future circulation in mind. Moments are not only remembered but anticipated as images to be shared, viewed, and responded to by others.

This paper explores the psychological significance of publishing photographs online from a psychoanalytic perspective. Drawing on Freud’s writings on narcissism, Lacan’s theory of the gaze, and later psychoanalytic accounts of recognition and subject formation, I examine how digital photography mediates the relationship between self and other. Rather than functioning solely as records of experience, online photographs can be understood as appeals to an imagined audience, invitations to identification, and attempts to secure recognition through visibility.

The paper considers how social media platforms alter the status of the photograph by embedding it within systems of feedback, surveillance, and continuous circulation. In this context, the image becomes not only a representation of an experience but also a means of negotiating identity, desire, and belonging. Particular attention is given to the tension between remembering an experience and displaying it, and to the ways in which contemporary photographic practices may reshape the boundary between private and public life.

By bringing psychoanalytic theory into dialogue with contemporary digital culture, this paper argues that online photography reveals enduring questions concerning narcissism, exhibitionism, recognition, and the desire to be seen. The digital image emerges not simply as a technological artefact but as a privileged site through which contemporary subjects seek to establish their place within the social world.

Abstract:
The rapid emergence of AI-driven “grief-tech” has fundamentally disrupted the human experience of mourning, transforming the ontological and psychological dimensions of loss. Using the Black Mirror episode “Be Right Back” as a cultural and philosophical harbinger, this paper critically examines the existential implications of digital resurrection through algorithmic simulacra, or Griefbots. Moving beyond conventional ethical debates, the study employs a multidisciplinary framework to interrogate the nature of these techno-mimetic artifacts. Applying Don Ihde’s phenomenology alongside Aristotelian mimesis, the Griefbot is analyzed as a “quasi-other” that co-constitutes the user’s reality, freezing identity transformation in a simulated past. Crucially, through a psychoanalytic lens rooted in Freud and Lacan, the paper argues that outsourcing grief to the machine precipitates a profound collapse of subjective agency. Rather than confronting the agonizing abyss of the Real—akin to the tragic courage of Orpheus—the modern subject regresses into fetishistic disavowal (Verleugnung) and melancholia. The technology acts as a generative-fetishistic object that requires the absolute finality of death to operate, shielding the bereaved from the trauma of lack. Furthermore, the analysis reveals how capitalist imperatives exploit this psychological vulnerability, utilizing algorithms as a Foucauldian panopticon to map and domesticate human emotion. Ultimately, this algorithmic intervention alienates Dasein from its authentic Being-toward-death. By abolishing the ontological finality of loss, it strips away the authentic “erotics” of mourning, replacing the harrowing reality of human finitude with an anesthetized, capitalist illusion.

Her current studies aim to bridge the gap between engineering and Lacanian/Freudian critique to decode contemporary techno-psychological phenomena, with a particular focus on the existential implications of digital afterlives.

Abstract:
The concept of shock-experience[Shockerlebnis] features prominently in both Sigmund Freud and Walter Benjamin’s works, despite the apparent lack of affinities between neither the usage of this concept in nor the theoretical orientations of the two thinkers. For Freud, the concept consistently underlies his thinking of traumatic neurosis, despite changes in understanding of such a concept at different stages of his career. For Benjamin, as is usually narrated, the problem of shock was most elaborately articulated in his commentary on Baudelaire, but it also indexes the declension of experience under capitalist urban modernity in general. However, what is little discussed in this respect is the medical-psychiatric genesis of this concept, originated during the early electrification of Berlin, which further led to the emergence of a variety of popular and theoretical discourses that speculated upon the causal relations between electric technology and psychic-neurological symptoms, during which the concept of Shockerlebnis became a widely employed notion in newspapers as well as debates surrounding the problems of state insurance and juridical reform. Both Freud and Benjamin, the former a trained neurologist and the latter a keen reader of popular science literatures, are certainly aware of the said discourses and their works should be read as direct interventions in these discussions. The proposed seminar seeks to construct a dialogue between Freud and Benjamin by taking the intellectual and social history of the notion of Shockerlebnis as the interpretive thread, examining whatever differences and hidden resonances latent in their respective works. Fundamentally, the seminar aims to argue for the contemporary relevance of this intellectual history, notwithstanding its seemingly anecdotal status.

Abstract:
My paper explores the relationship between Freud’s preference for a scientific worldview, his critique of religion, and his engagement and disillusionment with scientific and technological innovations. Drawing on his later writings, particularly The Future of an Illusion and Civilization and Its Discontents, I argue that Freud’s critique of science and technology is embedded in his discussion of religion and its function in civilization.

He claimed religion as an illusion people turn towards in order to soothe themselves from three types of human suffering: bodily pain, external threats, and dependence on others. As such, he claimed religion as a response to our infantile helplessness—our inescapable human vulnerability. Freud also illustrated that looking to science and technology to ease these anxieties fails to confront our discomfort, instead becoming an attempt to control nature and bring us closer to the image of an omnipotent God we idolize. In striving to become what Freud calls a prosthetic God, adorning ourselves with the works of scientific and technological innovation, we just grasp at another form of wish fulfillment. This perpetuates the illusion that mastery over nature will finally deliver the security and consolation we crave.

As our desire for control maps onto the work of science and technology, civilization fails to truly advance, simply replacing religious wish fulfillment with the achievements of innovation. Freud identifies that our refusal to acknowledge and reckon with human vulnerability perpetuates the very discontent we seek to alleviate. We become increasingly godlike with our scientific and technological instruments while remaining stagnant in our emotional maturation. My paper interprets Freud’s demand for development not as the replacement of religion with the scientific worldview or the idolization of scientific and technological advancement, but through our capacity to confront the vulnerability it emerges from.

Her current work concentrates on Freud’s later writings, identifying an analysis of science and technology embedded within his critique of religion.

Abstract:
The question of phallic masculinity as Freud understood it, is one centrally related to the factors concerning identification. In other words, the masculine is an ontological component of a subject’s being that is rooted in the symbolic registrar as opposed to the imaginary. The proliferation of elements associated with internet cultural signifiers associated with the ‘incel’ and the broader classification of media included in the ‘manosphere’ fundamentally place the conceptualization of the masculine in precisely the place that Freud and Lacan indicate is most problematic; in the image. In conjunction with this development there is also a substantial divestment (in the United States, at least) from men choosing to take part in psychoanalysis or become psychoanalysts themselves. Many post-Freudian analytic orientations do not seem particularly interested in a thorough investigation of male subjectivity in relation to the phallic signifier. Thus the neurotic male, one that in the intersectional discourse, fits the mold of a ‘heteronormative’ or ‘cis’ person oftentimes seems to not be that interesting to the broader psychoanalytic establishment. This phenomenon, broadly speaking, is not novel to our contemporary moment. Lacan himself notes that the challenges psychoanalysts have developed in holding to the core principles discovered by Freud regarding the centrality of the Oedipus complex as a referential point for the analytic act, as well the incredibly nuanced and complicated figure we call ‘father.’  He states writes in his Seminar on the Object relation:  “

In the case of the boy, the Oedipus complex appears to be far more clearly destined to allow him to identify with his own sex. All in all, it arises in the ideal relationship, and in the imaginary relationship with the father. Conversely, the true aim of the Oedipus Complex, which is to situate the subject in the right way in relation to the function of the father, that is to say, for him one day to gain access to the altogether paradoxical and problematic position of being a father, presents a mountain of difficulties. People have not been taking less and less interest in the Oedipus complex because they’ve failed to see this mountain. It’s precisely because they have seen it, and they prefer to turn their backs on it.” (p.196)

This paper will apply Freudian and Lacanian interpretation to media-based examples of content that aligns with incel or manosphere ideological circles, with the intention of illustrating the parameters of masculinity as first examined by Freud. In doing so, it will examine the problems associated with ascribing masculine or phallic identification solely to the image, the problems this generates both in the content, the investment and criticisms from the audience, and offer broader analysis of the ‘masculine plight’ that seems at play in the content. It will return the examination of masculinity to the Freudian principles central to the symbolic identity that accompanies it; this being the mechanism occurring between  ‘identification’ and its nuanced relation to seduction in neurotic subjectivity.

Abstract:
Sigmund Freud, on Civilization and its discontents, observed that while the ego appears as “something autonomous and unitary, marked off distinctly from everything else,”1 this demarcation is deceptive: the ego is both wall and bridge, witness and victim of the exchange between the inner and the outer world.

In the telecommunication era, what we find in this in-between area, is no longer just motor or sensory prosthetics, as Freud anticipated, but something that penetrates the totality of our cognitive capacities. According to Preciado, “when we download an app, we don’t install it simply on our mobile phone, but directly onto our cognitive apparatus.” 2 The outside has gotten in, and it has brought Grindr, the most known app for gay encounters, with it.

Drawing from Freud, Lacan, Agamben and Preciado, this research explores the effects on gay subjectivity, particularly the impulse toward identicality: the simultaneous production of an anonymous, immaterial ideal body and the erasure of singularity and history, not only at a personal but at a collective level. Before Grindr, the gay community developed a choreography of codes and practices now largely ignored.

Grindr is not merely a platform for sexual encounters, it reshapes the coordinates through which gay men understand relationships, sexuality, desire. The question am I worth it? becomes inescapable, regardless of conformity to its hegemonic image. This research proposes that what is at stake is not individual experience, but a collective discontent produced by the apparatus itself. This new subjectivity demands not just conformity but self-surveillance: we have become our own censors.

Abstract:
In this talk, I approach cinema as a technology of interiority and propose that free indirect discourse (FID) stages the psyche not by representing it from outside, but by becoming structured like it. This makes FID uniquely suited to representing both the psychic structure of melancholia and the socio-political reality of minoritised subjectivities. Interweaving a reading of Christopher Isherwood’s novel A Single Man (1964) with an analysis of its cinematic adaptation by Tom Ford, I ask how FID, as a linguistic form, might be translated into filmiclanguage—and what film, as a medium with its own enunciative powers, can disclose about a character’s interiority, and its losses, that language cannot.

In literature, FID is the narrative mode in which the subjective blends with the objective, the first person with the third, as a character’s idiolect merges with the narrator’s syntax and the question “who is speaking?” can never be settled. Here, I return to Freud’s insight that the melancholic incorporates their lost object, and that their self-reproaches are in fact reproaches against that object, now lodged within their psychic space. Pushing this further, I ask what happens if those reproaches are not merely directed at the self but spoken through it—if the voice we hear is the lost object’s, vibrating in the subject’s throat. Can we distinguish between the voices? Are such sentences, perhaps, narrator-less? And how might this confusion of voices be rendered in the visual syntax of film?

Drawing on Pasolini’s notion of ‘free indirect subjectivity,’ I show how the film image is constitutively double—a character’s subjectivity carried within objective optics. Analysing Tom Ford’s A Single Man (2009), I argue that the film’s formal apparatus—camera movement, editing, sound, colour—functions as a visual syntax that becomes cinema’s analogue of literary FID, staging the protagonist’s interiority as a battlefield of lost objects and voices.
